strengths: Addresses an important and timely systems problem: serving full-precision MoE models on memory-constrained edge devices without lossy quantization. The motivation around UMA-based platforms, SSD I/O bottlenecks, and batch-size-one inference is clear and practically relevant.

The core idea is technically appealing: exploit low-entropy BF16 exponent bits with lossless compression, cache different tensor components separately, and overlap SSD reads with CPU decompression and GPU reconstruction. This is a sensible co-design for the target hardware.

The evaluation covers three representative MoE models, two Jetson AGX Orin configurations, multiple memory budgets, batch sizes, and metrics including TPOT, TTFT, throughput, and end-to-end latency. The reported gains over SSD-offloading baselines are large and consistent.

The paper includes useful ablations for cache management and presents algorithmic details plus theoretical analyses for scheduling and cache planning, which helps clarify the intended behavior beyond a pure engineering prototype.
Because the compression is lossless, the work has a strong practical advantage over quantization-based deployment when exact model behavior is required.
weaknesses: The evaluation, while extensive on Jetson devices, is narrower than the paper’s broader claims about mobile and edge platforms. It does not evaluate phones, Apple Silicon, Raspberry Pi-class devices, different SSDs, thermal/power constraints, or concurrent mobile workloads, all of which could materially affect the proposed overlap and contention assumptions.

Baseline treatment is not fully convincing. The baselines are mostly run in default SSD-offloading modes, and the paper does not provide enough tuning detail to rule out configuration disadvantages. It also omits or only discusses related systems such as SwapMoE, KTransformers/Fiddler-style CPU-GPU hybrid inference, and recent MoE offloading/prefetching systems as direct empirical competitors.

Reproducibility is limited. The manuscript reports implementation size and hardware/software versions, but does not provide code, exact configurations, prompts/sample counts, random seeds, run counts, variance/error bars for most headline results, or enough detail to reproduce the compression/caching setup exactly.

Several claims are stronger than the evidence. The phrase “semantically lossless” is justified by lossless weight reconstruction, but the paper does not explicitly demonstrate bit-exact output equivalence across the full runtime path, including the GPU reconstruction kernel and interaction with framework execution.

The theoretical guarantee relies on simplified scheduling assumptions such as deterministic I/O/decompression costs, a single I/O thread model, fixed task costs, and idealized work-conserving behavior. These assumptions are not empirically stress-tested, and the cache-pool planning uses a heuristic makespan estimator despite the surrounding maximum-entropy formalism.

The limitations and ethics discussion is very thin. The impact statement is generic, and the paper does not discuss deployment risks such as increased local misuse capability, privacy/security tradeoffs of on-device LLMs, energy consumption, thermal behavior, or robustness under adversarial/workload-shifted expert activation patterns.

Presentation is generally clear but has many formatting and grammar issues, including missing spaces, awkward phrasing, and dense figures with small labels. These do not obscure the main idea, but they reduce polish and make some technical details harder to verify.

strengths: The paper targets a practically important problem: serving MoE LLMs on memory-constrained edge/mobile platforms without changing model weights or outputs through lossy quantization.

The high-level idea of exploiting BF16 exponent-bit redundancy together with compression-aware caching is sensible, and the paper gives useful motivation for why SSD I/O dominates on Jetson-style UMA devices.

The system design is reasonably complete at a conceptual level, combining offline bit-field decomposition, compressed tensor storage, hierarchical cache pools, asynchronous CPU decompression, and GPU tensor recovery.

The evaluation reports substantial latency and throughput gains over several general offloading baselines across three MoE models, and includes some ablations for cache planning and eviction policies.
weaknesses: The main performance claims are not yet convincingly supported. The strongest improvements are measured against broad offloading frameworks such as Accelerate and DeepSpeed, while several more directly relevant on-device or MoE-serving systems cited in the paper, such as SwapMoE, EdgeMoE, D2MoE, Fiddler, and KTransformers, are not evaluated. This makes the state-of-the-art comparison incomplete.

The evaluation is narrow for the breadth of the claims. Both testbeds are variants of Jetson AGX Orin with the same SSD class, and the workloads are sampled from ShareGPT only. The paper claims broad applicability to mobile and edge platforms, but does not test phones, Raspberry Pi/Apple-style SoCs, different storage devices, different OS memory pressure, or realistic concurrent mobile workloads.

Several theoretical components appear weak or disconnected from the implemented system. The scheduler proof relies on simplified homogeneous I/O/decompression costs, ignores GPU recovery and runtime contention, and contains questionable steps such as claiming a constructed schedule lower-bounds optimal idle time. The resulting constant-factor bound is also loose and does not seem to explain the empirical gains.

The cache planning model makes strong independence and stationarity assumptions about expert activations using rank-based marginal probabilities. These assumptions are not empirically validated, and the maximum-entropy argument does not show that the modeled distribution matches real prompt-dependent MoE routing behavior.

Reproducibility is inadequate. The manuscript does not provide code availability, exact model revisions, prompt lengths, generation parameters, number of prompts/runs, warmup procedures, statistical variability beyond a few shaded plots, profiler settings, SSD/page-cache control details, or enough configuration detail to reproduce the reported memory budgets and baselines.

The reported results need stronger statistical treatment. Most graphs lack confidence intervals or significance analysis, and the text emphasizes best-case ranges such as very large speedups without clearly separating typical gains, failure modes, and cases where baselines may be poorly configured or memory-budget control is coarse.

The paper under-discusses important systems costs and constraints, including offline compression time, metadata overhead, fragmentation, cache rebuild costs, sensitivity to compression backend and chunk size, CPU energy/power, thermal throttling, and interference with other mobile workloads.

Presentation has multiple rough edges and overclaims. The manuscript repeatedly states that ZipMoE shifts inference from I/O-bound to compute-centric and gives provable guarantees, but the evidence and theory only support this under restricted assumptions. There are also notation issues and typos in the algorithms and appendices, including overloaded symbols and undefined variables.

The impact statement is essentially boilerplate. Since the work can affect deployment of powerful LLMs on private edge devices, the paper should discuss energy, privacy, misuse, and risks from easier local deployment rather than saying no consequences need highlighting.

Overall, the idea is promising for a systems venue, but the ICML submission falls short on evidential strength, reproducibility, and technical rigor. The contribution is not mature enough to accept in its current form.

strengths: The paper identifies a timely and practically important problem: serving MoE LLMs on edge/UMA devices where expert offloading becomes dominated by SSD I/O rather than GPU compute. The motivation is convincing and supported by hardware measurements contrasting server and Jetson-style deployments.

The core idea is strong: exploit lossless compressibility of BF16 exponent fields and combine it with compression-aware caching and cache-affinity scheduling. This is a meaningful systems contribution because it preserves model weights exactly while targeting the actual bottleneck in on-device MoE serving.

The evaluation is broad for a systems paper: three representative MoE models, two Jetson AGX Orin configurations, multiple memory budgets, TPOT/TTFT, throughput, end-to-end latency, and cache-management ablations. The reported gains over Accelerate, DeepSpeed, and MoE-Infinity are large and consistent in the tested setting.

The design is well decomposed and mostly clearly presented, with a coherent offline compression pipeline, runtime DAG abstraction, hierarchical cache pools, and scheduler. The paper also provides algorithmic details and theoretical statements for the scheduling approximation and cache-hit modeling.

The contribution is original relative to typical lossy quantization/offloading work: it reframes MoE expert loading as a lossless compression plus CPU-parallel reconstruction problem, which is especially appropriate for UMA edge platforms.
weaknesses: Reproducibility is only partial. The paper reports implementation size and major dependencies, but does not specify code release, exact runtime configurations, cache grid settings, prompt counts, input/output length distributions, warmup protocol, number of trials, variance beyond Figure 9, or all baseline tuning details. These omissions make it hard to independently validate the large speedups.

The baseline comparison may understate stronger systems baselines. Accelerate and DeepSpeed in default SSD-offload modes are not necessarily optimized for Jetson edge inference, and MoE-Infinity is designed for different hardware assumptions. The paper would be stronger with careful tuning details, comparison to recent on-device MoE systems such as EdgeMoE/D2MoE where possible, and an ablation isolating compression from scheduling and cache planning across all models.

The theoretical analysis is ambitious but not fully convincing as written. Several proof steps rely on informal scheduling arguments, idealized task models, average profiled costs, and independence assumptions that are later approximated in Algorithm 3. The constant-factor scheduling guarantee therefore feels only loosely connected to the actual implementation and measured system behavior.

The evaluation scope is still narrower than the claims about mobile and edge platforms. Both main testbeds are NVIDIA Jetson AGX Orin devices with NVMe SSDs; there is no phone-class SoC, Apple Silicon, Raspberry Pi, eMMC/UFS storage, or non-NVIDIA GPU backend. Thus the generality to mainstream mobile deployment remains plausible but not established.

The paper does not include a substantive limitations section. Important limitations include dependence on BF16 exponent redundancy, SSD/page-cache behavior, availability of CPU cores during concurrent mobile workloads, model architecture assumptions, offline conversion overhead/storage format compatibility, and cases where lossy quantization may be acceptable or superior.

The ethics/impact statement is boilerplate and too dismissive. Since the paper motivates lossless inference partly through security risks of quantization and targets private on-device deployment, it should discuss privacy benefits, energy/battery implications, possible misuse from easier local deployment, and the limits of preserving weights exactly as a safety guarantee.

strengths: The paper targets an important and timely systems problem: serving MoE LLMs on memory-constrained edge devices without lossy quantization. The motivation is convincing, especially the analysis that UMA edge platforms shift the bottleneck toward SSD I/O and leave CPU resources underutilized.

The core idea is technically appealing: exploit low-entropy BF16 exponent fields with lossless compression, cache different tensor components separately, and overlap decompression with I/O through a cache-affinity scheduler. This is a useful systems contribution rather than just an engineering tweak.

The evaluation covers three MoE models, two Jetson AGX Orin configurations, several memory budgets, and multiple metrics including TTFT, TPOT, throughput, end-to-end latency, ablations, page-cache isolation, distribution-shift sensitivity, offline initialization cost, and compressor choice. The reported gains over Accelerate, DeepSpeed, and MoE-Infinity are large.
The paper includes nontrivial algorithmic modeling, including a scheduler approximation result and a maximum-entropy cache-planning derivation, which helps clarify the assumptions behind the design.

The method is lossless at the parameter representation level, so the paper plausibly avoids the behavioral changes introduced by quantization or pruning; this is a meaningful practical advantage for safety-sensitive on-device deployments.
weaknesses: Reproducibility is weaker than expected: the abstract says the code is available but the link is blank, and the paper does not provide enough implementation detail to independently reproduce the full C++/CUDA runtime, cache manager, or baseline configurations. This is a material issue for a systems paper with large empirical claims.

Hardware generality is not fully established. Despite claims of applicability to shared-memory platforms broadly, the main experiments are only on NVIDIA Jetson AGX Orin variants with one SSD type. There is no validation on phones, Raspberry Pi-class devices, Apple Silicon, or heterogeneous-memory systems, so the scope of the claims should be narrowed.

The baseline comparison may be incomplete or not sufficiently tuned. The main baselines are generic/offloading systems, while several closely related on-device or MoE-specific systems cited in the paper are not compared in the main evaluation. DeepSpeed is described as having coarse memory control, but it is unclear whether each baseline is optimized to the same degree as ZipMoE.

Some of the reported gains appear to depend partly on OS page-cache behavior and low-level implementation effects. The paper does include a page-cache isolation study, which is good, but the methodology for controlling cache state, warm-up, prompt counts, run-to-run variance, and statistical confidence is not described in enough detail.

The theoretical analysis is somewhat idealized relative to the implemented system. It assumes simplified latency models, profiled constants, a single I/O thread, and structured DAG tasks; the cache planning then uses a heuristic makespan approximation. The connection between the proved bounds and observed end-to-end behavior is therefore suggestive rather than decisive.

The lossless correctness claim would be stronger with explicit bit-exact validation, checksum tests, or output-equivalence tests across all models and compression backends. The paper asserts preservation of model behavior but does not show a direct correctness audit.

Limitations and ethics are thin. The discussion mentions hardware generalizability and compressor extensibility, but does not adequately discuss deployment constraints such as SSD wear, energy/power/thermal effects, memory pressure from real mobile apps, privacy implications of local cached model shards, or failure modes under adversarial/rapidly shifting routing distributions.

strengths: The paper targets an important practical problem: serving MoE LLMs on edge/shared-memory devices without lossy quantization. The motivation that MoE offloading becomes I/O-bound under tight memory budgets is plausible and relevant.

The core idea of exploiting low-entropy BF16 exponent bits with lossless compression, then coordinating decompression, tensor recovery, and cache management, is technically interesting and reasonably original as a systems contribution for MoE inference.

The manuscript includes a concrete prototype, multiple MoE models, two Jetson AGX Orin memory configurations, several baselines, ablations of cache management, page-cache isolation, sensitivity to workload shift, and an appendix with scheduling/cache-planning details.

The lossless nature of the approach is a real strength: if implemented correctly, it preserves model behavior while reducing storage/I/O, which is attractive for deployments where quantization risk is unacceptable.
weaknesses: The empirical support is not convincing enough for the strength of the claims. The paper claims broad applicability to mobile and edge platforms, but evaluation is limited to NVIDIA Jetson AGX Orin variants with the same SSD class. There is no phone, Raspberry Pi, Apple Silicon, integrated mobile NPU/GPU, or heterogeneous-memory evaluation, so the hardware-generalization claims are overextended.

Baseline methodology is under-specified and potentially unfair. The baselines are described as using default SSD offloading modes, but it is unclear whether MoE-Infinity, DeepSpeed, Accelerate, and FineMoE were carefully tuned for the target devices. Some reported gaps are extremely large, making this particularly important. FineMoE is only relegated to appendix tables and appears catastrophically slow, with little diagnosis beyond a brief explanation.

Reproducibility is weak. The abstract says code is available but provides no URL. Important details are missing or hard to recover, including exact prompt lengths, generation settings, number of samples, variance/statistical treatment, cache warm-up policy, SSD/page-cache control, per-baseline configuration, and how memory budgets are enforced across systems.

The evaluation mixes system effects in a way that obscures attribution. The authors acknowledge gains from OS page cache, GPU memory management, and low-level framework optimizations, but the ablations do not cleanly isolate compression, scheduling, cache planning, kernel recovery, and implementation engineering. This makes the central algorithmic contribution harder to assess.

The theoretical guarantees appear disconnected from the implemented system. The approximation analysis relies on a simplified DAG/workload model with offline-profiled constant costs, while the implementation combines E-chunk read and decompression for OS page-cache affinity and operates under real SSD/cache interference. The paper does not validate that the theorem meaningfully predicts runtime behavior.

The presentation is polished in broad strokes but has several issues: missing code link, occasional formatting/spacing errors, dense figures whose numerical values are difficult to read, and limited discussion of failure modes such as workloads with weak expert skew, compressed exponent distributions unlike the tested models, or memory pressure from real concurrent applications.

The ethics/impact statement is essentially boilerplate and dismissive. Given the paper motivates lossless inference partly through security risks of quantization and targets on-device deployment, it should discuss privacy, device resource contention, energy/battery impact, and risks of making larger models easier to deploy locally.

Overall, the paper has a promising systems idea and some useful evidence, but the central performance and generality claims are not yet supported with sufficient methodological rigor or reproducibility for acceptance at the main track.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and timely systems problem: serving MoE LLMs on memory-constrained edge/mobile platforms without changing model behavior through quantization or pruning. The focus on UMA-style shared-memory devices is well motivated and distinguishes the work from server-oriented MoE offloading systems.

The technical idea is compelling: decompose BF16 tensors into low-entropy exponent bits and high-entropy sign/mantissa bits, apply lossless compression to the exponent stream, and combine this with compression-aware cache tiers and asynchronous scheduling. This is a neat match between statistical redundancy in weights and the hardware profile of edge SoCs.

The evaluation is broad enough to support the main efficiency claim within the studied setting: three MoE models, two Jetson AGX Orin configurations, several memory budgets, batch sizes, and output lengths, with comparisons to Accelerate, DeepSpeed, MoE-Infinity, and an appendix comparison to FineMoE. Reported gains in TPOT, TTFT, throughput, and end-to-end latency are substantial.

The paper includes useful ablations and stress tests, including cache strategy comparisons, page-cache isolation under artificial background RAM pressure, compressor comparisons, offline initialization costs, and sensitivity to activation-distribution shifts. These strengthen the case that the gains are not solely due to opportunistic OS caching.

Because the compression is lossless, the claim of preserving model behavior is more credible than in quantization-based systems, and the paper correctly frames this as a practical advantage for security- or behavior-sensitive deployments.

The system description is relatively complete, including implementation size, compression backends, zero-copy/pinned-memory choices, cache planning, and a scheduler with a stated approximation guarantee.
weaknesses: The reproducibility story is incomplete. The abstract says code is available, but the manuscript text shows a blank code URL. For a systems paper with many implementation-sensitive optimizations, missing or unavailable code, scripts, and configuration details materially weaken reproducibility.

The empirical generality is narrower than the claims sometimes imply. The evaluation is conducted only on NVIDIA Jetson AGX Orin 64GB/32GB devices with one SSD class; broader statements about mobile phones, Raspberry Pi, Apple Silicon, and shared-memory platforms are plausible but not demonstrated.

Baseline treatment leaves some uncertainty. The main baselines are run in default SSD-offloading modes, but it is not fully clear whether each was carefully tuned for this unusual edge setting. The FineMoE comparison appears only in the appendix and reports extremely poor latency, which raises questions about configuration fairness or implementation compatibility.

Some performance gains are entangled with low-level system effects such as page cache behavior, GPU memory management, and framework optimizations. The paper does include an isolation experiment, but a more systematic breakdown of compression, scheduling, cache hierarchy, kernel recovery, and OS effects would make the causal attribution cleaner.

The theoretical scheduler guarantee is interesting but rests on a simplified task model with profiled fixed I/O/decompression costs and assumptions about work-conserving execution. The connection between this model and real hardware variability, page-cache hits, SSD contention, and CUDA scheduling is not fully validated experimentally.

The limitations and ethics discussion are thin. The paper briefly discusses hardware generalizability and compressor extensibility, but does not deeply address cases where lossless compression is less effective, when CPU contention with user applications is high, thermal/power constraints on mobile devices, or deployment risks from making larger MoE models easier to run locally.

Presentation is generally clear but has polish issues: several spacing/formatting errors, an empty code link, and some overstrong phrasing such as “first” and broad hardware-agnostic claims that should be qualified.
